title: Youth mental health decline is being framed as cumulative social pressure requiring prevention across school, family, work, housing, and digital life
source_unit: OECD, Child, Adolescent and Youth Mental Health in the 21st Century
geography: OECD countries, with comparable time-series, national data, expert interviews, and country examples including Canada, Korea, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and the United States

denominator.unit: OECD countries with comparable youth mental-health time series

decline_pattern.value: in 9 of 11 countries, youth mental-health indicators declined by an annual average of 3% to 16%

pandemic_boundary.value: COVID-19 intensified pressures, but the underlying decline was already visible from the mid-2010s

international_signal.value: between 2014 and 2022, the share of adolescents reporting frequent low mood and multiple health complaints increased in every HBSC-participating OECD country

recovery_uncertainty.value: some countries show early stabilization or partial recovery in 2023-2024, but durability is not yet established

observations.method: OECD cross-country synthesis of national surveys, international data series, administrative indicators, scientific evidence, and semi-structured interviews with clinical and policy experts.
observations.uncertainty: Measures and time coverage vary across countries; reported trends do not establish a single cause or prove that the same intervention would work across settings.
observations.subgroup: Children, adolescents, and young adults under 25, with attention to age, sex, socioeconomic status, school context, housing, digital exposure, and access to support.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some changes may reflect improved recognition, reporting, or service contact rather than only worsening underlying mental health; the report treats measurement improvement as necessary for interpretation.

denominator.unit: countries included in the reported self-harm hospitalisation comparison for girls aged 0-17

girl_outcome.unit: percent increase in self-harm hospitalisations among girls aged 0-17

age_sex_pattern.value: girls and older adolescents show particularly poor mental-health outcomes

suicide_boundary.value: suicide rates among young people remained relatively stable in most countries despite worsening distress indicators

driver_interaction.value: digitalisation, economic insecurity, school pressure, bullying, climate anxiety, conflict, and information exposure can accumulate rather than operate in isolation

observations.method: Synthesis of administrative and survey indicators with scientific evidence and expert interpretation; selected indicators are not a universal measure of all youth mental-health outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: Hospitalisations capture severe or service-contact events and are affected by access, coding, care-seeking, and system capacity; they do not measure all self-harm or distress.
observations.subgroup: Girls and young women, older adolescents, youth exposed to poverty, unstable housing, academic pressure, bullying, harmful online content, climate anxiety, or conflict information.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher recorded hospitalisation can reflect improved detection or access to care as well as greater incidence; the pattern should not be read as a single digital-media effect.

denominator.unit: clinical and policy experts interviewed for the report

causal_frame.value: experts and scientific evidence do not identify one factor; youth face multiple intersecting pressures that accumulate across domains

protective_environments.value: positive family relationships, supportive schools, secure housing, social connection, social-emotional learning, and mental-health literacy are identified as protective conditions

service_gap.value: existing support often relies too heavily on high-threshold clinical responses after difficulties escalate

preferred_response.value: low-threshold, holistic, community-based, and peer-supported services are prioritized for early assistance

observations.method: Expert interviews combined with literature review and comparative policy analysis; expert judgment is used to identify interacting risks and promising response directions.
observations.uncertainty: Expert consensus and promising models do not establish comparative causal effectiveness; implementation quality, reach, and subgroup fit remain open questions.
observations.subgroup: Young people who disengage from traditional services, youth facing multiple stressors, families with limited time or resources, schools, community organizations, and peer-support networks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Expanding services without addressing poverty, housing, school pressure, discrimination, and digital environments may medicalize structural distress without reducing its sources.

data_coverage.value: fewer than one-third of OECD countries collect regular, nationally representative time-series data on youth mental health

measurement_gap.value: digital-use measures remain coarse and many countries lack detailed data on socioeconomic vulnerability, school environments, and service access

policy_testing.value: school phone bans, age verification, and social-media restrictions are expanding while their mental-health effects remain mixed or unclear

accountability_route.value: better monitoring is needed to track trends, evaluate policies, and understand young people’s lived experience

observations.method: OECD assessment of national monitoring systems and emerging digital-policy interventions.
observations.uncertainty: The country-coverage estimate concerns regular nationally representative time series and does not mean that other data sources do not exist; data availability is not itself proof of policy failure.
observations.subgroup: Young people, parents, educators, health and social-service providers, policymakers, and groups whose experiences are missed by coarse digital, socioeconomic, or administrative measures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rapid policy experimentation may generate useful learning if interventions are proportionate, transparent, youth-informed, and evaluated for unintended effects rather than treated as settled solutions.

related_sources.claim: Official OECD 88-page report PDF with trends, drivers, responses, country comparisons, and data limitations.
Official OECD DOI and publication citation.

boundary: This record adds a youth mental-health-to-social-capacity route. It is not a respondent-level pooled dataset, a universal prevalence estimate, a causal attribution to digital media or COVID-19, or an evaluation proving that low-threshold services, school policies, or platform restrictions improve outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official OECD executive summary and report PDF were reviewed for the decade trend, 11-country time-series frame, 13-country self-harm comparison, 29 expert interviews, intersecting risk framework, prevention recommendations, digital-policy uncertainty, and monitoring gap.
